title: A Method for Generating Semantically Opaque Interface Identifiers with IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC)
summary: Describes how a host can build the host-specific half of its IPv6 address so that it stays the same within one network but changes when the host moves to another network. This is an alternative to deriving the address from the hardware (MAC) address, which would let people track a device everywhere. It keeps the benefits of stable addresses without the privacy cost.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7217 specifies how IPv6 hosts can create stable interface identifiers without embedding a hardware address. The identifier stays the same for an interface on a subnet, but normally changes when the host uses a different prefix, making it harder to track the host across networks.

questions: how to generate ipv6 interface identifiers
how to generate stable ipv6 interface identifiers
how does ipv6 avoid tracking by mac address
subtitle: A way to give IPv6 devices stable addresses on one network without carrying the same identifier everywhere.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 interface identifier based on a hardware address can expose device information and let observers correlate a host across networks.
tldr.mechanism: A host runs a pseudorandom function over its network prefix, interface identifier, optional network identifier, duplicate-address counter, and secret key, then takes bits from the result.
tldr.outcome: The identifier stays stable for an interface and prefix but changes across prefixes. The method replaces other stable SLAAC identifier-generation methods while allowing temporary addresses alongside it.

today: RFC 7217 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2014. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Hardware-Based Identifiers Cause Problems
sections.content:
Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) combines a network prefix advertised by a router with an Interface Identifier (IID) to form an IPv6 address. Traditional methods often derive the IID from a hardware address. The result can remain constant across networks, allowing activity to be correlated and exposing information about the device.

Predictable address patterns can also reduce the work needed to scan for hosts. Temporary addresses reduce some tracking, but traditional stable addresses may still be used for incoming connections and other functions. This RFC specifies a way to improve stable addresses whether or not temporary addresses are used.
sections.plainLanguage: A hardware-based identifier can reveal a device's network hardware and remain recognizable as the device moves. RFC 7217 replaces that identifier with one based on a secret calculation, while keeping the address stable on the same subnet.

sections.title: How the Method Fits with Other Addressing
sections.content:
The method is designed for SLAAC, but the RFC says it can also be used with DHCPv6 or manual address configuration. It improves stable addresses and can be used alongside the temporary addresses specified by RFC 4941.

The RFC does not change SLAAC itself or formally deprecate existing IID-generation methods. Existing address lifetime and renumbering behavior still apply. The method is incrementally deployable because nodes that do not use it have no interoperability change.
sections.plainLanguage: This method changes how a host creates a stable IPv6 identifier, not how SLAAC works. It can be used with temporary addresses, and nodes that do not use it can continue to operate normally.

sections.title: What the Identifier Must Achieve
sections.content:
For the same interface, prefix, and subnet, the method aims to produce the same IID. A different prefix should produce a statistically different IID, making it difficult for an observer to determine whether two addresses came from the same host. An outsider should also find the result difficult to predict, even after seeing other identifiers from the host.

Depending on the chosen interface identifier source, the result can be independent of the network hardware. The method applies to stable global, link-local, and unique-local IPv6 addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The same interface should keep its identifier on the same subnet. A different prefix should produce a different identifier that outsiders cannot readily predict.

sections.title: How a Host Generates an Identifier
sections.content:
A conforming implementation MUST use the specified algorithm to generate stable SLAAC identifiers. It computes RID = F(Prefix, Net_Iface, Network_ID, DAD_Counter, secret_key), then takes the needed bits from the least significant end of the result. The pseudorandom function F() must be hard to compute without the secret key and hard to reverse; it SHOULD output at least 64 bits. The RFC identifies SHA-1 and SHA-256 as possible choices and says MD5 is unacceptable.

The prefix comes from a Router Advertisement or is the link-local prefix. Net_Iface identifies the interface and must remain stable across system starts and network events, while differing for interfaces in simultaneous use. Network_ID is optional subnet-specific data. DAD_Counter starts at 0. The secret key SHOULD be at least 128 bits, must be initialized to a pseudorandom value, and should be restricted to this purpose.

The IID should be checked against reserved values and identifiers already in use. Implementations SHOULD allow an administrator to enable or disable the method. Appendix A discusses choices for Net_Iface, including interface indexes, interface names, link-layer addresses, and logical network service identities; each has different stability properties.
sections.plainLanguage: The host combines the network prefix and interface identity with optional network data, a conflict counter, and a secret key. It uses a pseudorandom function to produce the identifier, so the same inputs produce a stable result without exposing the hardware address.

sections.title: Handling Duplicate Addresses
sections.content:
If Duplicate Address Detection finds that a tentative address is already in use, the host SHOULD increase DAD_Counter by 1 and generate another identifier. It SHOULD wait a random amount of time between 0 and IDGEN_DELAY seconds before retrying, to reduce simultaneous retries by multiple hosts. Hosts SHOULD try at least IDGEN_RETRIES addresses, but MUST set a limit on attempts.

Hosts MAY save the counter for a particular prefix, interface and network tuple in non-volatile memory. If the conflict cannot be resolved, address configuration fails. A host MUST NOT automatically switch to another identifier-generation method. The specified defaults are 3 retries and a delay of 1 second.
sections.plainLanguage: If another host already uses the address, the device changes the counter and tries a new identifier. It must stop after a limited number of attempts, and it must not silently switch to a different generation method.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Limits
sections.content:
The method reduces simple tracking between networks, address scanning based on predictable identifiers, and disclosure of hardware addresses. Different prefixes produce different identifiers, so learning one stable identifier does not reveal the identifiers for other prefixes. Whether an address remains unchanged after hardware replacement depends on the chosen Net_Iface source.

An attacker on the same subnet might send a forged Router Advertisement and learn an identifier for a chosen prefix. RA-Guard may block the forged advertisement; an unknown optional Network_ID can make the learned value differ from the one used on the legitimate network. The RFC says a host should consider SEND if this attack is a concern. The secret key must remain protected because the method's privacy depends on its secrecy. This method complements rather than replaces temporary addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The method makes identifiers harder to use for tracking and scanning, but it does not remove every attack. Keep the secret key protected, and use the additional protections described by the RFC when forged router messages are a concern.
